posts.content_md:
Reading Saxby and this forum, I was under the impression that fiber had to be 6um (for red) to maintain coherency. In the Shoebox book, Frank recommends a specific type from Edmund, which I ordered. To my surprise, it turned out to be the unjacketed fat guage stuff you see in cheap lighted flower displays. Well, I went ahead and cut and bundled it as described in the book, shoved it up the D&S diode case, and gave it a shot (I love film... no worries about wasting a plate!). It actually worked! My question is, why? The image was relatively bright, but a little spotty, due to the 'dirty' ends of the fiber (cut by hand, no polishing). 

The details are as follows: The setup was Denisyuk, 2 inch sq PG-01 film between glass, with 3 stacked die as a subject. The fiber came on a roll, and maintained a curl that I couldn't relax, so it looked something like a half-moon crescent after cutting. 8 strands were cut to about 15 inches and bundled together. Since the fiber was unjacketed, light was bleeding everywhere out of the sides, which surprised me since I thought that fiber was supposed to *contain* the light completely. Nevertheless, the beam exited out of the ends of the fiber with that classic 'coherent speckle' reflecting off the subject it was illuminating, although it was a little dirty. Normally, my ideal exposure with the D&S is about 1.5 - 2 seconds for a 2 inch sq emulsion, but since I guessed that I was losing a ton of light efficiency, I increased it to 15 seconds. The result was a slightly under-exposed image, but much brighter than I expected. Why did this work with such a large guage (and curled for that matter)? Was is because of the single beam geometry? Would it fail if I split off half the fibers and routed them past the plate toward the object? Did the short length have anything to do with it?

posts.post_subject: Tried Defreita's fiber optic experiment last night....
posts.content_md: Off the top of my head, I'd guess your laser had a pretty good coherence length. If your laser is polarised, the extra time could also be the result of de-polarisation. When the beam goes through the fiber, the light bounces around inside and there is loss at each bounce, depending on the index of fiber/cladding. If, as you say, there was no cladding, then the surprise is that the light stayed in the fiber at all! A lot of these clading-less fibers are used to bleed light out of the edges to create "lines of light" along the fiber length. Anyway, the number of bounces means that the path length of the beam is uncertain to an extent (there is an equation that gives the path length inside the fiber as a function of the fiber length). So, firstly, you need to havve a laser with a long enough coherence length. Also, the fiber depolarises, so that the light coming out of the end is not polarised the same way as the light going in. However, the thinner the fiber, the more it maintains polarisation. Also, the thinner the fiber, the less the actual bouncing. The light travels through the fiber as a sort of "field" (A Bessel function of sorts). These thin fibers are called "single mode" and are very thin - on the order of a few microns.

Well, it does for the reflected light. I was thinking about brewsters windows in a laser and their function is to polarize the light. 

But in researching I found that at brewsters all reflected light is polarized in the P direction but is only about 15% of the total light. The transmitted light contains all the S polarized light and about 85% of the P polarized light. So I guess the way brewsters work in a laser is the constant passing back an forth through the brewsters continually filter out the P polarization until what is left is mostly S polarization. This makes sense because my windows are cut top to bottom and the polarization that comes out of my laser is S or Up and Down polarization.

[http://www.nebhe.org/photonIIsite/Brewsters_Angle.pdf](http://www.nebhe.org/photonIIsite/Brewsters_Angle.pdf)

SO this would not be so good for a single cut brewsters on a fiber end.

posts.content_md:
I guess the simplest although not the cheapest would be to use Polarization Maintaining fiber. 

> **http://www.ozoptics.com/ALLNEW_PDF/APN0005.pdf:** To solve this problem, several manufacturers have developed polarization maintaining fibers (PM fibers).These fibers work by inducing a difference in the speed of light for two perpendicular polarizationstraveling through the fiber. This birefringence creates two principal transmission axes within the fiber,known respectively as the fast and slow axes of the fiber. Provided the input light into a PM fiber islinearly polarized and orientated along one of these two axis, then the output light from the fiber willremain linearly polarized and aligned with that axis, even when subjected to external stresses.

I just thought of something. If the fiber optics were used just for object lighting then polarization would not even need to be worried about. Case in point. For a single beam reflection or H1 transmisison. Split the beam as usual for reference and object lighting. For the reference beam use a spatial filter as usual. For the object beam(s) lauch them into a single mode fiber cable with existing spatial filters and don't worry about polarization as the object reflects light to the plate unpolarized anyway. This will allow greater versitility in placement of object lighting and be especially usefull when changing to different objects.

Of course I have never tried this but it is very facinating and interesting. Grey good luck and keep us posted.

Of course I don't mind! You're thinking along the same track as I. A couple of things I recently found out:

Launching a beam into fiber via a direct diode connection isn't very expensive... around $400, but the connection needs to be tailor made for a specific wavelength. Splitters run about 200, but polarization maintaining splitters jump up to $1200, so your idea of splitting the off reference beam before hitting the launcher may be better. Another thing.. the couplers typically are only about 20 - 40% efficiency. In my case, my 25 mW diode would only emit 7 mW at the fiber output. And that's before splitting. 

As Saxby states, randomized polarization really only becomes an issue if the fiber run is stressed or too long, but that's only with a single run. There are no guarantees when running the beam through a non-PM splitter.

posts.content_md:
There was an airplane pilot named Bill Durrell who got the holography bug and took the Lake Forest workshops. He built and designed a contraption that would launch a laser into three separate fibers, all single mode, polarization-preserving. It used polarization type beamsplitters, and each fiber had its own alignment mechanism.

I got the pleasure of Beta-testing this thing. I had been shooting unslanted transmission gratings with each beam incident at 45 degrees to the plateholder. We plopped two of the fiber ends in front of the spatial filters, but they had to be fairly close.

Since incident flux was down from coupling losses, I adjusted the exposure to compensate. Developed nicely, but that's the only good thing to say about it. Shot some test strips bracketing up and down, but still nada.

Since I had just shot some kick a** bright gratings I knew the table and chemistry were OK. I put a Newport disc at the plateholder position and used it as a beam combiner, turning the set up into a Mach-Zehnder interferometer (rectangular layout as opposed to the + of the Michelson.)

The fringes were dancing around like crazy! The fibers weren't standing still for more than a couple of seconds!

So when Bill returned with the launcher he added sheaths to the fibers plus we clamped them to the table. This time it worked OK.

But we usually defaulted to using just one fiber in the Densiyuk mode. We even tried launching RGB lasers into three individual fibers and holding the ends in a common clamp, but even though the fibers are small, they do have finite dimension, so they were coming in a slightly different angles so there were colored edges to the shadows of objects.

Based on my experiences with fiber optics in holography I'd rather not. The spread needs to be controlled better; it comes out at an angle determined by the NA of the fiber, so to change the spread you need to put a lens after it, which makes another optic to keep clean, which is a waste since the light coming out of the fiber is as good as spatially filtered. Except you can't change the divergence as easily as changing an objective.

With polarization preserving fibers you need to be able to rotate the ends to align your vectors, not a big problem. And you have to work hard at alignment to keep your losses down.l But the worst part is the major battle with movement when there are more than one beam path because the fibers work by internal u]reflection[/u] which magnifies motion.

If anyone is interested, I can send you a pdf of Durrell's brochure by leaving a message in my mailbox on this forum. I believe that Graham does mention this device in some incarantion of his book.
